sheet.howExamined: C2 Higher only: 1 hour 15 minutes, 80 marks, calculator and Chemistry Data Leaflet allowed. Concentration and atom economy often share one quantitative question. A mass-of-solute or concentration calculation is [2] to [3], one mark for each line (moles, Mr, answer), and error carried forward means an early slip costs only its own line. An atom economy is [3]: the desired mass with its balancing number, the total mass of products, the percentage, sometimes set as 'show that'. A 'why is it (not) sustainable' or 'why is a high atom economy important' part is [1] to [2] and wants wasted atoms and cost. Other shapes: a concentration from a mass [1] to [2] (2021, 2026); moles in a volume [1] to [2], then what else is needed to find the mass (2022: the Mr).

noteBlocks.md: **Concentration** is the number of moles of dissolved substance, the **solute**, in each cubic decimetre (dm³) of solution. Its unit is **mol/dm³**, read as moles per cubic decimetre. The words that matter are *in each dm³*: a big bottle can hold more moles than a small one and still be weaker, because its moles are spread through more solution.

noteBlocks.title: The one line to learn
noteBlocks.md:
**concentration (mol/dm³) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution (dm³)**
It is a share: the moles divided out over the dm³.

noteBlocks.stem: One beaker holds 0.090 mol of solute in 250 cm³ of solution. What is the concentration of the solution, and why is it not 0.090 mol/dm³? [2]

steps.working: 1000 ÷ 250 = 4, so 4 such beakers would fill 1 dm³.
steps.decision: Concentration is about each dm³, so first ask how many of these beakers make one.

steps.working: Each beaker holds 0.090 mol, so 1 dm³ holds 4 × 0.090 = 0.360 mol.
steps.decision: It is one solution throughout, so every beaker-full carries the same moles.
The moles in each dm³ is the concentration: the same whether you look at one beaker or the whole dm³.

steps.working: 0.090 mol is what the beaker holds, not what each dm³ holds: it says how much, not how strong.
steps.decision: The near miss. Pour the beaker into a bigger one with water and it still holds the same moles, but the solution is weaker.

noteBlocks.explain: Concentration is the moles in each dm³. 10 of these flasks fill 1 dm³, so 1 dm³ holds 10 × 0.019 = 0.190 mol, as steps 1 and 2 of See it did with 4 beakers: 0.190 mol/dm³. 0.019 is what the flask holds, not each dm³.

noteBlocks.md: Laboratory volumes are measured in cm³, but the formula needs dm³. A cubic decimetre is a cube 10 cm along each edge, so it holds 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³, one litre. So the first line of any concentration calculation converts the volume on its own: **divide cm³ by 1000**. The dm³ is the bigger unit, so the number always gets smaller.

noteBlocks.stem: A student measures 130 cm³ of one solution and 45.0 cm³ of another. Write each volume in dm³. [2]

steps.decision: A 10 cm cube holds 10 × 10 × 10 one-centimetre cubes.
Divide by 1000: there are fewer of the bigger unit.
Keep the zeros: three significant figures in, three out.
Multiplying goes back to cm³. If your dm³ number is bigger than the cm³ number, you multiplied by mistake.

noteBlocks.explain: A dm³ holds 1000 cm³, so there are a thousand times fewer dm³: divide by 1000, as step 2 of See it did. 84.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.0840 dm³. If you reached 84000, you multiplied.

twin.explain: Divide by 1000, as steps 2 and 3 of See it did: 3200 ÷ 1000 = 3.20 dm³. The dm³ is the bigger unit, so the number gets smaller.

noteBlocks.text: 3. Why chemists count moles, not grams

noteBlocks.md: Reactions happen particle by particle, and one mole of any substance is the same number of particles. So two solutions with the same concentration in mol/dm³ carry the same number of solute particles in every dm³, ready to react, even when the masses dissolved are very different. That is why CCEA asks for mol/dm³.

noteBlocks.title: Why grams per dm³ would mislead
noteBlocks.md: Two solutions with 10 g in each dm³ look equally strong. But 10 g of a substance with light particles is more moles than 10 g of one with heavy particles, so the first would react with more.

noteBlocks.stem: Lithium hydroxide, $\ce{LiOH}$, and potassium hydroxide, $\ce{KOH}$, are each made up as 0.175 mol/dm³ solutions. Compare 1 dm³ of each. [3]

steps.working: Each holds 0.175 mol of solute in 1 dm³: the same number of particles.
steps.decision: Equal mol/dm³ means equal moles in equal volumes; that is what the unit says.
mass = moles × Mr, with Mr LiOH = 7 + 16 + 1 = 24 and KOH = 39 + 16 + 1 = 56.

steps.working: Same moles, different masses: each dm³ can neutralise the same amount of acid.
steps.decision: The moles decide how much can react; the grams only show how heavy each particle is.

noteBlocks.prompt: Sodium chloride and potassium chloride solutions are both 0.800 mol/dm³. What is the same in 1 dm³ of each?
options: the number of moles of solute
the mass of solute
the mass and the moles of solute
noteBlocks.answer: the number of moles of solute
noteBlocks.explain: Equal mol/dm³ means equal moles in each dm³, step 1 of See it. The masses differ because the Mr values differ, 58.5 for sodium chloride and 74.5 for potassium chloride, as step 2 showed for the two hydroxides.

optionNotes.why: The labels match, so it is tempting to think the grams do too, but a potassium chloride particle is heavier, so a dm³ of it holds more grams.

optionNotes.option: the mass and the moles of solute
optionNotes.why: Only half true: the moles match, but the masses cannot, because the two salts have different Mr values, 58.5 and 74.5.

twin.prompt: Copper(II) sulfate and zinc sulfate solutions are both 0.700 mol/dm³. Which statement about 1 dm³ of each is true?
options: they hold equal numbers of moles of solute
they hold equal masses of solute
the zinc sulfate holds more moles, because its Mr is bigger
twin.answer: they hold equal numbers of moles of solute
twin.explain: The label says mol/dm³: equal moles in every dm³, step 1 of See it. The heavier zinc sulfate puts more grams in the dm³, not more moles.

optionNotes.option: they hold equal masses of solute
optionNotes.why: Equal concentrations in mol/dm³ mean equal moles; the masses differ because zinc sulfate has the larger Mr.

optionNotes.option: the zinc sulfate holds more moles, because its Mr is bigger
optionNotes.why: A bigger Mr makes each mole heavier, not more numerous: the label says 0.700 mol in every dm³ of both.

noteBlocks.md: When the moles are given, a concentration takes two lines. **Line 1:** the volume in dm³. **Line 2:** concentration = moles ÷ volume. Each line is a mark, so write both even when the arithmetic feels easy, and give the unit, mol/dm³. Dividing by the volume in cm³ gives an answer a thousand times too small.

noteBlocks.stem: 0.066 mol of potassium iodide is dissolved in water to make 275 cm³ of solution. Calculate its concentration in mol/dm³. [2]

steps.decision: Convert first, on a line of its own: it is a mark of its own.
Moles over dm³. Dividing by 275 instead gives 0.00024, a thousand times too small.

noteBlocks.prompt: 0.063 mol of solute is dissolved to make 450 cm³ of solution. What is its concentration in mol/dm³?
noteBlocks.explain: Two lines, as in See it: the volume first, 450 ÷ 1000 = 0.450 dm³ (step 1), then moles ÷ volume, 0.063 ÷ 0.450 = 0.140 mol/dm³ (step 2).

twin.prompt: 0.052 mol of solute is dissolved to make 325 cm³ of solution. What is its concentration in mol/dm³?
twin.explain: Volume first, 325 ÷ 1000 = 0.325 dm³, then 0.052 ÷ 0.325 = 0.160 mol/dm³, steps 1 and 2 of See it.

noteBlocks.caption: The mass goes in as grams; the concentration counts moles, so the grams become moles first.

noteBlocks.md: Most questions give a **mass** of solute. Concentration counts moles, so the grams become moles first: **moles = mass ÷ Mr**, with the Mr built from the Data Leaflet's relative atomic masses. That is a line of its own and a mark of its own. Then carry on as before: the volume in dm³, then moles ÷ volume.

noteBlocks.stem: 2.38 g of potassium bromide, $\ce{KBr}$, is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³. [3]

steps.decision: The volume first, as always.
Mass ÷ Mr turns grams into moles. Dividing the grams by the volume would give grams per dm³, not moles.
Moles over dm³, with the unit.

noteBlocks.prompt: Lithium chloride, LiCl, has Mr 42.5. How many moles are there in 5.10 g of it?
noteBlocks.explain: Grams become moles by dividing by the Mr, step 2 of See it: 5.10 ÷ 42.5 = 0.120 mol. Dividing 42.5 by 5.10 gives 8.3, the fraction upside down.

twin.prompt: Potassium iodide, KI, has Mr 166. How many moles are there in 2.49 g of it?
twin.explain: Moles = mass ÷ Mr, step 2 of See it: 2.49 ÷ 166 = 0.0150 mol.

noteBlocks.md: Turn the formula round when the concentration is known: **moles = concentration × volume (dm³)**. If the question wants grams, add one more line: **mass = moles × Mr**. That is the Higher three-mark shape: the moles, the Mr, then the mass, a mark for each.

noteBlocks.stem: Calculate the mass of ammonium nitrate, $\ce{NH4NO3}$, needed to make 180 cm³ of a solution of concentration 0.450 mol/dm³. [3]

steps.decision: Concentration × volume in dm³: 180 cm³ is 0.180 dm³.
Count every atom: two nitrogens, four hydrogens and three oxygens.
Moles × Mr gives grams. Leaving the volume as 180 gives 6480 g, a sign to go back to step 1.

noteBlocks.prompt: How many moles of solute are in 35.0 cm³ of a solution of concentration 0.900 mol/dm³?
noteBlocks.explain: Concentration × volume in dm³, step 1 of See it: 35.0 cm³ = 0.0350 dm³, so 0.900 × 0.0350 = 0.0315 mol. Multiplying by 35.0 gives 31.5 mol, far too many for a small beaker.

twin.prompt: How many moles of solute are in 70.0 cm³ of a solution of concentration 0.550 mol/dm³?
twin.explain: Concentration × volume in dm³, step 1 of See it: 0.550 × 0.0700 = 0.0385 mol.

noteBlocks.md: You never need three separate formulae. Concentration is defined as the moles shared out over the dm³, so the other two come from undoing that sharing, the way you rearrange any equation: multiply both sides by the volume, or divide both sides by the concentration.

noteBlocks.stem: Starting from the definition of concentration, show how to find the volume of solution that holds a given number of moles. [2]

steps.decision: The definition: the moles, n, shared over the volume, V, in dm³.
Multiply both sides by V: the moles in any volume.
Divide both sides by c: the volume that holds n moles.

steps.working: Check: 0.0810 ÷ 0.450 = 0.180 dm³, the 180 cm³ of section 6.
steps.decision: Put known numbers back in: the ammonium nitrate solution returns its own volume.

noteBlocks.prompt: What volume of a 0.210 mol/dm³ solution contains 0.0189 mol of solute? Give your answer in cm³.
noteBlocks.explain: Volume = moles ÷ concentration, step 3 of See it: 0.0189 ÷ 0.210 = 0.0900 dm³, and × 1000 gives 90.0 cm³. The formula gives dm³, so convert back when cm³ is asked.

twin.prompt: What volume of a 0.140 mol/dm³ solution contains 0.0154 mol of solute? Give your answer in cm³.
twin.explain: V = n ÷ c, step 3 of See it: 0.0154 ÷ 0.140 = 0.110 dm³, which is 110 cm³.

noteBlocks.md:
Most reactions make something besides the product you want. **Atom economy** measures how much of the total mass of products is the product you want:
**atom economy = (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100**
It comes from the **balanced equation** alone. Mass is conserved, so the products weigh what the reactants weighed, and a by-product carries its share away as waste.

noteBlocks.title: What atom economy is not
noteBlocks.md: Percentage yield is the near miss. Yield comes from an experiment: the mass you collected over the most you could have made. Atom economy comes from the equation, and it stays the same however carefully you work.

noteBlocks.stem: Magnesium carbonate is heated: $\ce{MgCO3 -> MgO + CO2}$. A student could make at most 4.00 g of magnesium oxide and collects 3.30 g. (a) Calculate the atom economy for making magnesium oxide. (b) Explain why 82.5% is not the atom economy. [4]

steps.decision: The product you want, from the equation.
Every product, the carbon dioxide included. It equals the 84 of the carbonate, because mass is conserved.
Desired over total, times 100.

steps.working: (b) 3.30 ÷ 4.00 × 100 = 82.5% is the percentage yield: collected over the most possible.
steps.decision: Yield comes from the experiment; atom economy from the equation. Collecting every gram would not change the atom economy.

noteBlocks.md: In a balanced equation the big numbers multiply whole formulae, so they multiply masses too. The desired mass is its Mr times its balancing number, and so is every product in the total. Leave one out and the percentage is wrong. A free check: the reactants' total equals the products' total, because mass is conserved.

noteBlocks.stem: Zinc oxide is made by roasting zinc sulfide in air: $\ce{2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2}$. Calculate the atom economy for making zinc oxide. Give your answer to one decimal place. [3]

steps.decision: The 2 in front belongs to the zinc oxide, so it doubles its mass.
SO₂ = 32 + (2 × 16) = 64, and the equation makes two of them.
One decimal place, as asked: 55.862 is 55.9.
Equal totals, so no balancing number has gone missing.

noteBlocks.prompt: Boron is made from boron oxide and magnesium: B₂O₃ + 3Mg → 2B + 3MgO. What is the atom economy for making boron, to one decimal place?
noteBlocks.explain: Every mass carries its balancing number, steps 1 and 2 of See it: the boron is 2 × 11 = 22 and the products total 22 + (3 × 40) = 142, so 22 ÷ 142 × 100 = 15.5%. Leaving out the 3 in front of MgO gives 35.5%.

twin.prompt: Silicon is made by heating silicon dioxide with carbon: SiO₂ + 2C → Si + 2CO. What is the atom economy for making silicon, to one decimal place?
twin.explain: The 2 in front of CO doubles its mass, step 2 of See it: total 28 + (2 × 28) = 84, so 28 ÷ 84 × 100 = 33.3%.

noteBlocks.text: 10. Why a high atom economy matters

noteBlocks.md:
A full answer gives two separate reasons.
**Sustainable development:** fewer raw materials are used up to make the same product, and less waste is made.
**Economic:** less money is spent on raw materials that end up as waste, and on getting rid of that waste.
Argue from the atoms, never from energy or speed.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2025 C2 Higher Q5
noteBlocks.md: Asked why a laboratory preparation with a low atom economy was **not sustainable**, candidates struggled, and answers about **using less energy were not credited**. Argue from the atoms: raw materials used up, waste made, and what both cost.

noteBlocks.stem: A process makes its product with an atom economy of 35%. Give two reasons why the manufacturer would prefer a route with a higher atom economy. [2]

steps.working: 35% means 100 − 35 = 65% of the mass of the products is not the product wanted.
steps.decision: Start from the number: the rest is by-product, usually waste.

steps.working: Sustainable development: a higher atom economy uses up fewer raw materials and makes less waste for each kilogram of product.
steps.decision: One reason about resources and waste.

steps.working: Economic: less money is spent on raw materials that end up as waste, and on disposing of it.
steps.decision: A second, separate reason about money.

steps.working: Not: 'it uses less energy' or 'it is faster'. Atom economy says nothing about either.
steps.decision: The near miss the 2025 report names: energy was not credited.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is an economic reason for wanting a high atom economy?
options: less money is wasted on raw materials that become by-products
fewer of the Earth's resources are used up
less waste goes to landfill
noteBlocks.answer: less money is wasted on raw materials that become by-products
noteBlocks.explain: Economic means money; sustainable development means resources and waste. Step 3 of See it gave the money reason: less spent on raw materials that end up as waste. The other two are true, but they are the sustainable-development reason of step 2.

optionNotes.option: fewer of the Earth's resources are used up
optionNotes.why: A true reason, which is why it tempts, but it is the sustainable-development one: it is about resources, not money.
Also true, but less waste is a sustainable-development reason; the economic reason must be about money spent.

twin.prompt: Which of these is a sustainable-development reason for wanting a high atom economy?
options: less of the raw materials is turned into waste
the company saves money on waste disposal
the reaction uses less energy
twin.answer: less of the raw materials is turned into waste
twin.explain: Sustainable development is about resources and waste, step 2 of See it. Saving money is the economic reason, and energy earns nothing.

optionNotes.option: the company saves money on waste disposal
optionNotes.why: A real reason, but money makes it the economic one; the sustainable reason is about raw materials and waste themselves.
Atom economy says nothing about energy: it comes from masses in the equation, and the 2025 report says energy was not credited.

noteBlocks.md:
**'Show that the atom economy is …'** (2025). The value is printed, so the marks are for the lines: the desired mass, the total mass, the division. End on more figures than the value given, then round.
**'What else would you need?'** (2022). Given a concentration and a volume, the missing piece for a mass is the relative formula mass.

**'Give your answer to one decimal place'** (2022). The accuracy mark needs exactly one place: 38.0, not 38.
**'Dissolved in … cm³ of water'** (2026). Take the volume given as the volume of the solution, and convert it as usual.
**'Not sustainable'** (2025). A low atom economy means most of the mass is waste and raw materials are used up; energy earns nothing.

steps.decision: The product wanted, from the Data Leaflet's masses.
Water is the by-product: 2 + 16 = 18.

steps.working: 74.5 ÷ 92.5 × 100 = 80.54%, which is 80.5% to one decimal place.
steps.decision: End on more figures than the value printed, then round: typing the printed value back shows nothing.

noteBlocks.text: 12. Going further: both halves in one question

noteBlocks.md: Higher papers set both halves in one question (2022, 2025): a solution to make up, then an atom economy to calculate and judge. Nothing new is needed, only the order and the care: the moles and the mass first, then the equation's masses, each on its own line. The chain below works both halves on one substance.

noteBlocks.title: Where the specification stops
noteBlocks.md: Every concentration on your paper is in mol/dm³. Concentrations in g/dm³, titration calculations and gas volumes are not on this specification.

noteBlocks.stem: Potassium sulfate is made by $\ce{2KOH + H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + 2H2O}$. (a) Calculate the mass of potassium sulfate needed to make 280 cm³ of a 0.0700 mol/dm³ solution. [3] (b) Calculate the atom economy for making potassium sulfate, to one decimal place. [3]

steps.decision: Concentration × volume in dm³ first.
Two potassiums: the 2 is inside the formula.
Moles × Mr.
The Mr from part (a) is the desired mass: no need to work it again.
The 2 in front of the water doubles its mass.
82.857 to one decimal place.

noteBlocks.prompt: The same 0.0700 mol/dm³ potassium sulfate solution is used again. What mass of potassium sulfate is in 30.0 cm³ of it, in grams?
noteBlocks.explain: Moles first, then mass, steps 1 and 3 of See it: 0.0700 × 0.0300 = 0.00210 mol, and 0.00210 × 174 = 0.365 g. The Mr is the 174 of step 2.

twin.prompt: What mass of potassium sulfate is in 15.0 cm³ of the same 0.0700 mol/dm³ solution, in grams?
twin.explain: Moles, then mass, steps 1 and 3 of See it: 0.0700 × 0.0150 = 0.00105 mol, and × 174 = 0.183 g.

noteBlocks.md:
Convert cm³ to dm³ first, then find a concentration as moles ÷ volume.
Turn a mass into moles with the Mr before finding a concentration.
Find moles as concentration × volume, and a mass as moles × Mr.
Calculate an atom economy with every balancing number, and show a given value.
Give a sustainable and an economic reason for a high atom economy, never energy.

This is Higher Tier only, and the two halves often share a question. A mass or a concentration is [2] to [3]: the volume in dm³, the moles, the Mr, the answer, each a line. An atom economy is [3]: desired mass, total mass of products, percentage, to the places asked. Write every line, because a slip is carried forward. For *not sustainable*, argue from wasted atoms and cost.

items.stem: What is the relative formula mass, Mr, of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃? (Na = 23, C = 12, O = 16)
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.7: relative formula mass. You are not expected to have met this lesson yet.

options.feedback: 2 × 23 + 12 + 3 × 16 = 106. Every Mr in this lesson is built the same way, one subscript at a time.
That counts one sodium. The subscript 2 after Na doubles it: 2 × 23 = 46, so the Mr is 106.
That counts one of each atom. Each subscript multiplies the atom before it: two sodiums and three oxygens.

items.stem: How many moles are there in 20 g of sodium hydroxide, NaOH (Mr = 40)?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.7: moles from a mass.

options.feedback: Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 20 ÷ 40 = 0.5. This lesson uses that line in almost every calculation.
That is Mr ÷ mass, the fraction upside down. Moles = mass ÷ Mr = 20 ÷ 40.
That multiplies the mass by the Mr. To go from grams to moles, divide by the Mr.

items.stem: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃ (Mr = 100)?
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.7: a mass from moles.

options.feedback: Mass = moles × Mr = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g.
That is Mr ÷ moles. From moles back to grams you multiply: 0.25 × 100.
That divides the moles by the Mr. Going from moles to grams, multiply by the Mr.

items.stem: What is the Mr of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂? (Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1)
items.skill: Prerequisite from C1 §1.7: a bracket in a formula.

options.feedback: 40 + 2 × (16 + 1) = 74. The 2 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside it.
That ignores the 2 outside the bracket. It doubles the whole OH group: 2 × 17 = 34.
Only the oxygen has been doubled. The 2 outside the bracket doubles the hydrogen as well.

items.stem: How many cm³ are there in 1 dm³?
items.skill: Know the conversion between cm³ and dm³

options.feedback: A cube 10 cm on each edge: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³.
That would be a square 10 cm by 10 cm, which is an area. A volume has three dimensions: 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.
A decimetre is 10 cm, but a cubic decimetre is 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 cm³.

items.stem: Which of these gives a concentration in mol/dm³?

options.feedback: Moles per dm³: the unit spells out the formula.
That is the fraction upside down. Read the unit: mol/dm³ is moles divided by dm³.
Multiplying gives nothing useful here. Concentration is moles shared out per dm³, so divide.

options.text: mass in grams ÷ volume in dm³
options.feedback: That gives grams per dm³. CCEA's unit is mol/dm³, so turn the mass into moles first.

items.stem: 0.200 mol of solute is dissolved to make 500 cm³ of solution. What is the concentration?
items.skill: Calculate a concentration, converting the volume

options.feedback: That divides by 500, the volume in cm³. Convert first: 500 cm³ = 0.500 dm³.
That is volume ÷ moles. Concentration is moles ÷ volume: 0.200 ÷ 0.500.
That multiplies the moles by the volume. Concentration divides: 0.200 ÷ 0.500.

items.stem: How many moles of solute are there in 20.0 cm³ of a solution of concentration 0.500 mol/dm³?
items.skill: Calculate moles from a concentration and a volume

options.feedback: That multiplies by 20.0, the volume still in cm³. Convert first: 20.0 cm³ = 0.0200 dm³.
That divides the concentration by the volume. Moles = concentration × volume.
That divides the volume by the concentration. Moles = concentration × volume.

items.stem: Solution P holds 0.10 mol in 250 cm³. Solution Q holds 0.30 mol in 1.00 dm³. Which is more concentrated?

options.text: P, because each dm³ of it holds 0.40 mol
options.feedback: 0.10 ÷ 0.250 = 0.40 mol/dm³ for P, against 0.30 mol/dm³ for Q.

options.text: Q, because it contains more solute
options.feedback: Q holds more moles, but spread through four times the volume. Concentration is moles per dm³: P has 0.40, Q has 0.30.
0.10 ÷ 250 uses the volume in cm³. In dm³, P is 0.10 ÷ 0.250 = 0.40 mol/dm³, which beats Q's 0.30.

items.stem: Which expression gives the atom economy for making a product?

options.text: (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100
options.feedback: The product you want, over everything the equation makes, as a percentage.

options.text: (total mass of products ÷ mass of desired product) × 100
options.feedback: Upside down: this always gives more than 100%, which is impossible for an atom economy.

options.text: (mass of desired product ÷ mass of by-products) × 100
options.feedback: The bottom line is every product, the desired one included, not the waste alone.
That is percentage yield, which needs an experiment. Atom economy comes from the balanced equation.

items.stem: Methane and steam make hydrogen: CH₄ + H₂O → CO + 3H₂. What is the atom economy for making hydrogen? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)

options.feedback: 3 × 2 = 6 of hydrogen out of 34 in total: 6 ÷ 34 × 100 = 17.6%.
That uses one H₂ instead of three. The balancing number 3 is part of the mass: 3 × 2 = 6.
That puts the carbon monoxide on top. The question wants hydrogen, so hydrogen goes on top.
Over 100% means the fraction is upside down: desired mass on top, total underneath.

options.text: fewer raw materials are used up and less waste is made
options.feedback: Both halves of the sustainability reason. The economic reason, lower costs, is the other mark.

Speed is rate, a different topic. Atom economy says nothing about how fast a reaction goes.

findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: the desired mass is right and the final line follows correctly from the total. The total is the mark that goes. Multiply every formula mass by its balancing number, and compare your product total with the reactant total before you divide.

Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The 2 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside it, so Ca(NO₃)₂ has two nitrogens and six oxygens: 40 + 2 × (14 + 48) = 164. prompts.prompt: Write the formula for concentration, with its units.
To change a volume in cm³ into dm³, you …
How do you find the moles of solute in a volume of solution of known concentration?
prompts.answer: Moles = concentration × volume, with the volume in dm³.

prompts.prompt: Write the formula for atom economy.
prompts.answer: Atom economy = (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100.

prompts.prompt: What is the atom economy of a reaction that makes only one product, and why?
prompts.answer: 100%, because every atom of the reactants ends up in the desired product.

prompts.prompt: Give one sustainable-development and one economic reason for a high atom economy.
prompts.answer: Fewer raw materials used up and less waste; less money spent on raw materials and waste.

prompts.prompt: Where does atom economy come from, and where does percentage yield come from?
prompts.answer: Atom economy from the balanced equation; percentage yield from an experiment.

prompts.prompt: An atom economy comes out above 100%. What has gone wrong?
prompts.answer: The fraction is upside down: desired mass on top, total mass of products underneath.

findings.asked: Calculate the mass of an acid needed to make 250 cm³ of solution of a stated concentration in mol/dm³.
findings.wentWrong: Candidates found it hard; most still picked up some marks because each line of their working was followed through.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Turned 250 cm³ into 0.250 dm³, multiplied by the concentration to get the moles, worked out the Mr from the Data Leaflet, and multiplied the moles by the Mr.
findings.rule: Three lines, each worth a mark: moles = concentration × volume in dm³; the Mr; mass = moles × Mr. Write all three so a slip costs one mark, not three.

findings.asked: Show that a laboratory preparation had a given atom economy from its balanced equation, then explain why the method was not sustainable.
findings.wentWrong: The calculation went well for a large share of candidates, but the explanation did not: many struggled, and answers about the method using less energy were not credited.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Multiplied the desired product's formula mass by its balancing number, added every product for the total, and then argued from the low atom economy: most of the mass wasted, raw materials used up, not cost effective.
findings.rule: Explain sustainability with atoms and money: raw materials used up, waste made, cost. Energy is a different argument and earns nothing here.

findings.asked: Calculate relative formula masses, one of them with a bracketed group.
findings.wentWrong: Mostly done well, but some candidates did not multiply the atoms inside the bracket by the number outside it, or added up the bracket wrongly.
findings.rule: Work out the bracketed group first, then multiply it by the number outside: Mg(NO₃)₂ is 24 + 2 × (14 + 48).

findings.asked: Calculate the percentage of iron in an iron(III) compound.
findings.wentWrong: Most succeeded, though a few counted iron once where the formula holds two iron atoms.
findings.rule: Every subscript multiplies the atom in front of it. Read Fe₂ as two irons before you add anything up.

insight.ruleToRemember: Convert the volume, then work in moles, one line per mark. For atom economy, multiply every formula mass by its balancing number and put the product you want over the total mass of all the products. Argue sustainability from wasted atoms and money, never energy.
insight.aStarSignal: An answer to 'why is this not sustainable' that quotes the atom economy it is arguing from, then names the raw materials used up, the waste made and the cost, in that order.
